In pairs, they classify examples (e.g. choosing a Head Teacher by the Ministry of Education, voting for a Ward Councillor, a King inheriting a throne) as elections or not, giving reasons based on the features discussed. Assessment criteria: learners correctly classify examples and justify their classification using the features of an election.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: in Mkushi District, candidates Mwansa and Chomba contest for Ward Councillor; registered residents queue at Chalata Polling Station, mark ballots in secret booths, drop them into sealed ballot boxes, and presiding officers count votes in the presence of party monitors, with Mwansa declared winner with 1,200 votes against Chomba's 950. Tasks: (a) explain the meaning of an election using the scenario [4 marks]; (b) identify three features of an election shown in the scenario [6 marks]; role-play task — re-enact the Chalata Polling Station scene with a presiding officer verifying voters, polling agents observing, voters queuing and marking ballots in secret, and the officer announcing the result. Expected answers: (a) an election is a formal, organised process in which registered citizens choose their leaders by casting votes [4]. (b) features shown: more than one candidate; registered voters; secret ballot voting booths; sealed ballot boxes and vote counting; presence of monitors for transparency (any three) [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners' answers correctly explain the meaning of an election and identify at least three accurate features from the scenario; the role-play accurately depicts an orderly, transparent polling process. Level of difficulty: (a) Understanding (b) Analysing; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to interview a parent or guardian about the last time they voted in Zambia (e.g. 2021 general elections, a council by-election, or a cooperative society election) and record what they remember about the voting process: (a) record what election the parent/guardian voted in and when [2 marks]; (b) record one feature of the voting process they described [3 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners conduct a short interview at home and record the findings in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit a written record showing they conducted the interview and identified a genuine feature of the voting process.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'An election is more than just marking a paper — it is an organised, fair process that gives every eligible Zambian a voice in choosing their leaders.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state, in one sentence, the meaning of an election. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly and confidently define an election.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.1 Elections — Establishing the Importance of Elections
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Establishing importance of elections
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to establish and explain the importance of elections in a democratic society such as Zambia.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, debate cards.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson deepens learners' appreciation of democracy by linking elections to accountability, participation and national development. It uses debate and real-life Zambian illustrations to build critical thinking. This is the 3rd lesson in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.1.1 Justify significance of electing leaders
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners know the meaning and key features of an election (previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher poses a provocative statement for a quick debate: 'Zambia would develop faster if the President were simply chosen by a group of wise elders instead of holding costly elections every five years.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners take a quick stance (agree/disagree) with a one-sentence reason; most disagree, arguing elders may not represent everyone's interests, while a few agree citing cost savings. Assessment criteria: learners engage with the statement and offer an initial, reasoned opinion.

progression.teacherRole: Explains that elections are important because they give citizens a voice in choosing who governs them, hold leaders accountable since they can be voted out, promote peaceful transfer of power, legitimise a government's authority, and allow citizens to influence policies affecting their lives. Real-life application: discusses how a Member of Parliament for Mkushi North who fails to fulfil campaign promises (e.g. on the Mkushi-Serenje road) risks losing the next election.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes. In groups, they are given a card with one importance of elections (e.g. accountability, legitimacy, peaceful transfer of power) and prepare a one-minute explanation supported by a relevant Zambian example, such as Constituency Development Fund projects tied to MP performance. Assessment criteria: learners collaborate effectively and present a clear, well-supported explanation of their assigned point.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: in Serenje District, residents are unhappy that their Ward Councillor has not repaired the community borehole for three years despite promises; community members remind each other that the next Local Government election is in a few months and agree to use their vote to decide whether he continues in office. Tasks: (a) state one importance of elections shown in the scenario [3 marks]; (b) explain how the scenario demonstrates that elections make leaders accountable [7 marks]; role-play task — dramatise a community meeting (insaka) in Serenje where residents confront the Councillor, remind him of the upcoming election, and he responds with a plan of action, including a Village Headperson moderating [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) elections give citizens power to hold leaders accountable and to remove non-performing leaders [3]. (b) because the Councillor knows the community can vote him out, he has an incentive to fulfil promises such as repairing the borehole; elections thus create pressure on leaders to perform, unlike appointed leaders who cannot be removed by those they serve [7].
progression.learnersRole: Learners' answers correctly identify and explain the accountability function of elections using the scenario; the role-play realistically portrays community accountability pressure on an elected leader. Level of difficulty: (a) Remembering (b) Analysing; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to discuss with a parent or elder one project or service in their own community (e.g. a clinic, road, school block) that was promised by an elected leader, and to record whether it was delivered: (a) record the project/service promised and by which elected leader [2 marks]; (b) record whether it was delivered, and one reason why elections matter in this case [3 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners engage a parent or elder in discussion and record findings in a short written note. Assessment criteria: learners submit a written note showing genuine engagement and a reasoned link to the importance of elections.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes that elections are the tool citizens use to reward good leadership and hold poor leadership accountable.
progression.learnersRole: Learners share one importance of elections they will remember. Assessment criteria: learners can state at least one clear importance of elections.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.1 Elections — Describing Characteristics of a Credible Election
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Describing characteristics of a credible election
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to describe the characteristics of a credible election and apply them to real Zambian scenarios.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, checklist cards.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson equips learners with standards for evaluating whether an election is trustworthy, developing analytical and critical thinking skills through Zambian case examples. This is the 4th lesson in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.1.1 Justify significance of electing leaders
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the meaning and importance of elections (previous lessons).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks whether learners would trust the result of a nearby chiefdom's cooperative society election if only the chairperson's relatives were allowed to vote, and why.
progression.learnersRole: Learners respond with their opinions, saying they would not trust it because not everyone was allowed to vote, making it unfair and unrepresentative. Assessment criteria: learners engage with the question and identify at least one reason for distrust.

progression.teacherRole: Explains that a credible election is one that is free, fair, transparent and widely accepted as legitimate, and lists characteristics: free participation without intimidation, fair and equal treatment of candidates, transparency in vote counting and results announcement, independence of the electoral body (e.g. the Electoral Commission of Zambia), secrecy of the ballot, and accurate results. Real-life application: notes that bodies such as the Churches Monitoring Group and the Commonwealth Observer Mission have monitored Zambian polls and declared them largely credible, boosting public confidence.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes on the characteristics. In groups, they are given a checklist card and a short case (e.g. a village cooperative election) and must tick which characteristics were present or absent, correctly justifying their assessment using case details. Assessment criteria: learners accurately apply the checklist of characteristics to the given case and justify their conclusions.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: during a Parent-Teacher Association (PTA) election at Chibombo Secondary School, all registered parents could nominate and vote, voting was by secret ballot, votes were counted in full view of parents present and results announced immediately; however, one parent later complained that the Chairperson had campaigned using threats against parents who supported his rival. Tasks: (a) identify two characteristics of a credible election shown in the scenario [4 marks]; (b) explain why the complaint raised threatens the credibility of the election [6 marks]; role-play task — dramatise a PTA disciplinary hearing investigating the intimidation complaint, with a panel comprising the Head Teacher, a Governing Body representative and two parents, culminating in a recommendation on safeguarding future PTA elections [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) secret ballot voting; transparent vote counting in front of parents; immediate and open announcement of results (any two) [4]. (b) the intimidation complaint shows some parents may not have voted freely, violating the principle that a credible election must be free from intimidation, undermining legitimacy even if other procedures like ballot secrecy were followed correctly [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly identify characteristics present and give a sound analytical explanation of the threat to credibility; the role-play demonstrates a fair, structured investigation process. Level of difficulty: (a) Remembering (b) Analysing; role-play: Evaluating.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to think of any election they have witnessed or heard about in their community (church, cooperative, market association) and assess it against the characteristics of a credible election learnt in class: (a) name the election observed and state one characteristic of credibility it met [3 marks]; (b) state one characteristic it may have lacked, if any [2 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners reflect on a real or reported election and record their assessment in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit a written assessment correctly applying at least one credibility characteristic to a real example.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'A credible election is not just about voting — it is about fairness, transparency and freedom from fear at every stage of the process.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners name one characteristic of a credible election they will remember. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly state at least one characteristic of a credible election.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.1 Elections — Classifying the Types of Elections (Presidential, National Assembly and Local Government)
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Classifying the types of elections (Presidential, National Assembly and Local Government)
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to classify the types of elections held in Zambia, namely Presidential, National Assembly and Local Government elections.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, chart showing Zambia's three-tier elective structure.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson helps learners distinguish between the three levels of elective office in Zambia's governance structure, developing analytical thinking through classification exercises using Zambianised examples. This is the 5th lesson in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.1.1 Justify significance of electing leaders
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the characteristics of a credible election (previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks: 'On the same voting day in Zambia's general elections, how many different leaders does a voter in Mkushi actually choose?'
progression.learnersRole: Learners try to recall and guess the number and names of positions, mentioning President, Member of Parliament and Councillor, though some may only recall the President. Assessment criteria: learners attempt to recall the positions voted for, applying prior general knowledge.

progression.teacherRole: Explains that Zambia holds three types of elections concurrently during general elections: Presidential election (Republican President and Vice-President running mate); National Assembly election (MPs for each of 156 constituencies); Local Government election (Councillors for each ward, and Mayors/Council Chairpersons in some councils, who oversee local development such as roads, markets and clinics). Real-life application: uses a chart to show a single Mkushi voter's three ballot papers on election day — one each for President, the MP for Mkushi North, and the Ward Councillor.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes, copying the chart. In pairs, they match given responsibilities (e.g. 'repairs the Chalata feeder road', 'represents Zambia internationally', 'makes laws') to the appropriate type of election/leader — matching the feeder road to the Councillor, international representation to the President, and law-making to the MP. Assessment criteria: learners correctly classify responsibilities under the appropriate type of election/leader.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: during the 2026 by-elections in Mkushi District, three separate ballot papers were used at Katanino Polling Station — a green ballot for the Republican President, a ballot for the MP for Mkushi North Constituency, and another for the Ward Councillor of Chalata Ward; first-time voter Chansa was confused about why she had to vote three times. Tasks: (a) classify the three types of elections shown at Katanino Polling Station [6 marks]; (b) explain to Chansa why Zambia holds three separate elections at once [4 marks]; role-play task — re-enact the scene at Katanino Polling Station with a presiding officer explaining to Chansa the purpose of each of the three ballot papers before she casts her three votes [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) Presidential election — for the Republican President; National Assembly election — for the MP for Mkushi North Constituency; Local Government election — for the Ward Councillor of Chalata Ward [6]. (b) Zambia holds three elections together because governance operates at three levels — national, constituency and ward — each with different responsibilities, and voting for all three at once ensures every level of government is filled and saves the cost of separate election days [4].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly classify all three types of elections and give a sound explanation for holding them concurrently; the role-play clearly demonstrates the distinct purpose of each ballot. Level of difficulty: (a) Remembering (b) Understanding; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to find out, from a parent, guardian or local newspaper, the names of the current MP for their constituency and the Ward Councillor for their area: (a) record the name of the MP for their constituency [2 marks]; (b) record the name of their Ward Councillor and one responsibility they hold [3 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners research at home and record findings in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit correctly recorded names and at least one accurate responsibility of the Councillor.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher draws three columns on the board — 'President', 'MP' and 'Councillor' — and asks the class to chorally state the level of government each represents (National, Constituency, Ward).
progression.learnersRole: Learners respond chorally, matching each leader to their level of government. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly and confidently classify the three types of elections and their corresponding levels of government.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.1 Elections — Analysing the Forms of Elections (General and By-elections)
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Analysing the forms of elections (General and By-elections)
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to analyse the difference between General Elections and By-elections in the Zambian context.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, newspaper report on a Zambian by-election.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson completes learners' understanding of Sub-topic 2.2.1 by distinguishing the two forms elections may take, using real Zambian by-election cases to build analytical skill. This is the 6th in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.1.1 Justify significance of electing leaders
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners can classify the types of elections in Zambia (previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks why Zambia sometimes holds an election for only one constituency, like Kaputa or Chilanga, outside the usual five-year general election cycle.
progression.learnersRole: Learners engage with the question and attempt a reasonable guess, such as that the previous MP died, resigned, or was removed from office. Assessment criteria: learners offer their guesses and engage with the question.

progression.teacherRole: Explains that a General Election is held nationwide at the end of a five-year term to elect the President, all 156 MPs and all Councillors at once, while a By-election is held in a single constituency or ward at any time to fill a vacancy arising before the next general election (e.g. due to death, resignation, or court-ordered removal of the sitting MP or Councillor). Explains common causes of by-elections in Zambia: death, resignation, adoption of foreign citizenship, court-ordered removal.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes on the two forms of elections, comparing them in a two-column table (General Election vs By-election) under headings such as scope, timing and cause, correctly noting a general election covers the whole country on a fixed five-year cycle while a by-election covers only one constituency/ward and can occur at any time. Assessment criteria: learners correctly complete the comparison table distinguishing the two forms of elections.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: in 2025 the MP for Mkushi North Constituency passed away suddenly, and the Electoral Commission of Zambia announced a by-election to be held within 90 days to elect a new MP for Mkushi North only, while residents of other constituencies continued to be represented by their sitting MPs elected in 2021 until the 2026 general election. Tasks: (a) identify the form of election that will be held in Mkushi North Constituency, giving one reason [4 marks]; (b) distinguish this form of election from a general election using details from the scenario [6 marks]; role-play task — dramatise an Electoral Commission of Zambia press briefing at Mkushi Boma announcing the by-election and explaining to journalists why only Mkushi North will vote and how the process differs from a general election [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) a by-election, because it is being called to fill a single vacancy created by the death of the sitting MP, rather than at the end of a nationwide five-year term [4]. (b) unlike a general election, which covers the whole country and elects the President, all MPs and all Councillors on a fixed five-year cycle, the by-election covers only Mkushi North Constituency, is called suddenly due to a vacancy, and does not affect other constituencies [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly identify and distinguish the two forms of elections using scenario evidence; the role-play accurately conveys the scope and cause of the by-election. Level of difficulty: (a) Understanding (b) Analysing; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to search a newspaper, radio bulletin or ask an elder about any by-election that has taken place in Zambia in recent years (e.g. Kwacha, Kaputa, Chilanga, or a local council ward): (a) record the name of the constituency/ward and the reason the by-election was called [3 marks]; (b) state one way this by-election differed from a general election [2 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners research at home and record findings in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit an accurate record of a real Zambian by-election and one correct point of difference from a general election.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'A general election renews the whole nation's leadership at once, while a by-election simply fills a single gap when it arises — both keep Zambia's democracy continuously representative.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state, in one sentence, the difference between a general election and a by-election. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly distinguish the two forms of elections.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.2 Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) — Describing the Role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Describing the role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to describe the role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) in organising, conducting and managing elections.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, picture/logo of the Electoral Commission of Zambia.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson introduces learners to Zambia's constitutional electoral management body, building citizenship awareness through Zambianised, real-life illustrations of ECZ's work. This is the 7th lesson in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.2.1 Analyse the role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ)
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the types and forms of elections in Zambia (previous lessons).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher shows the ECZ logo and asks who is responsible for making sure elections in Zambia run smoothly, from registering voters to announcing the winner.
progression.learnersRole: Learners guess and discuss; some correctly name the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ), others guess the police or the President. Assessment criteria: learners attempt a reasonable guess and engage with the picture.

progression.teacherRole: Explains that ECZ is the independent constitutional body responsible for organising, conducting and managing all elections and referenda in Zambia, and describes its key roles: registering voters and maintaining the voters' register, delimiting constituencies and wards, accrediting candidates and political parties, conducting voter education, and managing polling, counting and results. Real-life application: describes ECZ mobile teams visiting Mkushi Boma and surrounding chiefdoms to register new voters.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes on ECZ's roles. In groups, they match given activities (e.g. 'printing ballot papers', 'announcing results', 'campaigning for a candidate') to 'ECZ role' or 'not an ECZ role', correctly identifying printing ballot papers and announcing results as ECZ roles and campaigning as not. Assessment criteria: learners correctly classify activities as ECZ roles or not, with sound reasoning.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: ahead of the 2026 Mkushi North by-election, an ECZ mobile team set up a registration desk at Chalata Community Hall, verifying residents' National Registration Cards, capturing biometric details and issuing voter cards; on election day ECZ-appointed presiding officers managed the polling station, counted votes transparently, and announced results to party monitors present. Tasks: (a) describe two roles of ECZ shown in the scenario [4 marks]; (b) explain why it is important for ECZ, rather than a political party, to manage this process [6 marks]; role-play task — dramatise the ECZ mobile registration desk at Chalata Community Hall, with roles for a registration officer verifying an NRC, capturing biometric details, and issuing a voter's card to a first-time voter [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) roles shown — registering voters and issuing voter cards; managing the polling station, counting votes and announcing results [4]. (b) it is important for ECZ, as an independent and neutral body, to manage the process because a political party has an interest in the outcome and might manipulate registration or counting to favour its own candidate; ECZ's independence ensures the process is trusted by all candidates and voters [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly describe ECZ roles from the scenario and give a sound explanation of the importance of ECZ's independence; the role-play accurately depicts the registration process. Level of difficulty: (a) Remembering (b) Analysing; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to ask a parent or guardian whether they have ever registered as a voter with ECZ, and what the process involved: (a) record whether the parent/guardian has registered as a voter [2 marks]; (b) record one step of the ECZ registration process they described [3 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners interview a family member and record findings in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit a written record showing genuine engagement and at least one accurate registration step.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'From registering voters at Chalata to announcing results, the Electoral Commission of Zambia is the trusted referee that makes our elections fair and orderly.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state one role of ECZ they will remember. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly state at least one role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.2 Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) — Discussing the Electoral Process (Part 1: Legislation and Delimitation)
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Discussing the Electoral Process (Part 1: Legislation and Delimitation)
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to discuss the legislation and delimitation stages of Zambia's electoral process.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, map showing Zambia's constituency boundaries.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson splits the compacted 'Electoral Process' learning activity into a focused, manageable segment covering the legal framework and constituency/ward boundary-setting, using Zambianised examples. This is the 8th lesson in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.2.1 Analyse the role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ)
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks: 'Before any Zambian can vote, what rules and boundaries must first be set by law?'
progression.learnersRole: Learners brainstorm ideas, mentioning the Constitution, electoral laws, or boundaries of constituencies, though few know the specific terms. Assessment criteria: learners attempt to brainstorm relevant ideas about pre-election legal preparation.

progression.teacherRole: Explains that the electoral process begins with legislation — the laws governing how elections are conducted in Zambia, principally the Constitution of Zambia and the Electoral Process Act — and explains delimitation as the process of dividing the country into constituencies (for MPs) and wards (for Councillors) based on population size and geography, conducted periodically by ECZ. Real-life application: uses Mkushi North and Mkushi South Constituencies for National Assembly elections as an example of how delimitation creates manageable, fairly-sized voting areas.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes on legislation and delimitation. In pairs, they study a simplified map of Mkushi District's wards and constituencies and identify which ward/constituency they would vote in for a given village. Assessment criteria: learners correctly interpret the map and identify the appropriate ward/constituency.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: following growth of Mkushi Boma's population due to new settlements around Katanino, ECZ announced a delimitation exercise to review ward boundaries, guided by the Electoral Process Act; residents of the newly settled area were unsure which ward they now belonged to and attended a public consultation meeting organised by ECZ. Tasks: (a) explain the meaning of delimitation as shown in the scenario [4 marks]; (b) discuss why legislation such as the Electoral Process Act is necessary to guide delimitation [6 marks]; role-play task — dramatise the ECZ public consultation meeting at Katanino, with a delimitation officer explaining the new proposed ward boundary on a map and residents asking questions [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) delimitation is the process of dividing an area into constituencies/wards based on factors such as population; in the scenario ECZ is reviewing Mkushi's ward boundaries because the population around Katanino has grown [4]. (b) legislation such as the Electoral Process Act is necessary because it sets clear, legal criteria and procedures for how boundaries should be drawn (e.g. population thresholds, public consultation), preventing arbitrary or biased boundary changes and giving residents a legal right to be consulted [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly explain delimitation and the role of legislation using the scenario; the role-play accurately reflects a genuine public consultation process. Level of difficulty: (a) Understanding (b) Analysing; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to find out from a parent, guardian or local Councillor's office which ward and constituency their home area falls under: (a) record the name of their ward and constituency [2 marks]; (b) state one reason why it matters to know their ward/constituency [3 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners research at home and record findings in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit correctly recorded ward/constituency information with a sound reason.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'Before Zambians can even vote, the law must first set the rules, and delimitation must fairly draw the boundaries — the electoral process begins long before election day.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state one thing they learnt about legislation or delimitation. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly explain either legislation or delimitation in their own words.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.2 Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) — Discussing the Electoral Process (Part 2: Voter Education and Registration)
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Discussing the Electoral Process (Part 2: Voter Education and Registration)
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to discuss the voter education and voter registration stages of Zambia's electoral process.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, sample voter's card image.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson completes the electoral process learning activity by focusing on how citizens are prepared and enrolled to vote, using Zambianised community examples to develop communication and citizenship. This is the 9th lesson in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.2.1 Analyse the role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ)
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand legislation and delimitation stages of the electoral process (previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks why some people who are 18 years and above still fail to vote on election day.
progression.learnersRole: Learners brainstorm reasons such as not being registered, not knowing where to vote, or not understanding the importance of voting. Assessment criteria: learners engage and propose reasonable explanations.

progression.teacherRole: Explains voter education as the process by which ECZ informs citizens about their right to vote, how to register, how to vote correctly, and the importance of participating, and voter registration as the process by which eligible citizens (18+, holding an NRC) enrol their details in the voters' register. Explains ECZ's voter education methods: radio and television programmes, community meetings, school civic clubs, printed materials in local languages. Real-life application: describes how ECZ partnered with community radio stations such as Mkushi Community Radio to educate first-time voters ahead of the 2021 general elections.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes on voter education and registration. In pairs, they design a simple voter education message (a slogan or short jingle) in English or a local language encouraging first-time voters to register. Assessment criteria: learners produce a relevant and appropriately targeted voter education message.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: ahead of the 2026 by-election, Mkushi Community Radio aired a voter education programme in Bemba explaining eligibility, required documents and mobile registration desk locations in Chalata and Katanino Wards; many first-time voters, including 19-year-old Bwalya, listened and later went to register with their NRCs. Tasks: (a) distinguish between voter education and voter registration as shown in the scenario [4 marks]; (b) explain why voter education was necessary before Bwalya could register [6 marks]; role-play task — dramatise a voter education radio programme with a presenter interviewing an ECZ officer about eligibility and registration requirements, followed by a scene of Bwalya registering at the Chalata mobile desk [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) voter education is the radio programme informing citizens about eligibility, requirements and registration locations; voter registration is the actual process of Bwalya presenting his NRC and enrolling his details at the mobile desk [4]. (b) without voter education, Bwalya may not have known he was eligible, what documents were required, or where and when to register; voter education equips citizens with the knowledge and confidence to exercise their right to register and vote [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly distinguish voter education from registration and give a sound explanation of their relationship; the role-play accurately depicts both processes in sequence. Level of difficulty: (a) Understanding (b) Analysing; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to design, on paper, a short voter education poster (with a slogan and picture idea) that could be displayed at their local clinic, market or school to encourage eligible community members to register as voters: (a) draw or describe the poster design and slogan [3 marks]; (b) explain in one sentence why the poster's message matters [2 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners design a poster idea at home and present it in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit a relevant, well-explained voter education poster idea.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'An informed voter is an empowered voter — voter education opens the door, and registration is the key that lets every eligible Zambian walk through it on election day.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state one thing they learnt about voter education or registration. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly explain either voter education or voter registration in their own words.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.2 Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) — Describing the Electoral Code of Conduct
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Describing the Electoral Code of Conduct
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to describe the Electoral Code of Conduct and its role in guiding candidate and voter behaviour in Zambia.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, printed extract of Electoral Code of Conduct rules.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson helps learners understand the rules that regulate campaign behaviour, developing citizenship and emotional intelligence (self-control, respect for others) through Zambianised campaign scenarios. This is the 10th lesson in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.2.1 Analyse the role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ)
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand voter education and registration (previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks whether learners have ever seen or heard of political party supporters fighting or insulting each other during campaigns, and what rules should stop this.
progression.learnersRole: Learners share experiences and suggestions, recalling campaign clashes reported on radio/TV and suggesting rules against violence, insults or bribery. Assessment criteria: learners share relevant experiences and reasonable suggestions.

progression.teacherRole: Explains the Electoral Code of Conduct as a set of rules issued under the Electoral Process Act governing the behaviour of candidates, parties, supporters and voters during the electoral period, and outlines key rules: no violence, threats or intimidation; no abusive or inciting language; no bribery of voters (vote-buying); no misuse of government resources for campaigning. Real-life application: cites cases where ECZ, working with the Zambia Police Service, has warned or disqualified candidates for breaching the Code, such as political violence between rival cadres during campaign rallies.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes on the Code of Conduct rules. In groups, they are given short campaign scenarios and must decide whether the behaviour breaches the Code, giving a reason — correctly identifying threats or bribery against supporters as breaches, while normal rallies and door-to-door canvassing are acceptable. Assessment criteria: learners correctly distinguish acceptable campaign conduct from breaches of the Code.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: during campaigns for the Mkushi North by-election, one candidate's supporters distributed bags of mealie-meal to Chalata Ward residents in exchange for votes, and separately, supporters of two rival candidates clashed at a market in Katanino, exchanging insults and minor scuffles, before Police and ECZ monitors intervened. Tasks: (a) identify two breaches of the Electoral Code of Conduct shown in the scenario [4 marks]; (b) explain how such breaches can undermine the credibility of the by-election [6 marks]; role-play task — dramatise an ECZ and Zambia Police joint intervention at Katanino Market, separating the clashing supporters, cautioning them on the Code of Conduct, and recording witness statements about the mealie-meal distribution [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) breaches shown — vote-buying (distributing mealie-meal for votes); political violence/intimidation (clashes and insults between rival supporters) [4]. (b) vote-buying corrupts voters' free choice, making the result reflect gifts received rather than genuine support; violence and intimidation frighten voters and supporters away from participating freely, reducing turnout and fairness, and together these breaches can lead observers to question whether the result reflects the will of the people [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly identify breaches and explain their impact on credibility; the role-play realistically shows enforcement of the Electoral Code of Conduct. Level of difficulty: (a) Remembering (b) Evaluating; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to recall any campaign period they have witnessed (local or national) and identify one example of good conduct and, if any, one example of poor conduct they observed or heard about: (a) record one example of good campaign conduct observed [2 marks]; (b) record one example of poor conduct (if any) and why it was wrong [3 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners reflect on a real campaign period and record their observations in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit a thoughtful, relevant reflection distinguishing good and poor campaign conduct.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'The Electoral Code of Conduct is like a referee's rulebook — it keeps campaigns fair, peaceful and respectful for everyone.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state one rule of the Electoral Code of Conduct they will remember. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly state at least one rule of the Electoral Code of Conduct.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.2 Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) — Discussing Voters' Rights
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Discussing voters' rights
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to discuss the rights of voters in Zambia and how these rights are protected during elections.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, extract of the Bill of Rights relating to political participation.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson builds learners' awareness of their own future rights as voters, developing citizenship and communication skills through Zambianised scenarios of rights being upheld or challenged. This is the 11th lesson in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.2.1 Analyse the role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ)
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the Electoral Code of Conduct (previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks: 'If you turn 18 next year and go to vote, what would you expect to be entitled to as a voter?'
progression.learnersRole: Learners brainstorm expectations, mentioning the right to vote secretly, to vote without being forced, and to have their vote counted fairly. Assessment criteria: learners engage and propose reasonable expectations.

progression.teacherRole: Explains voters' rights as the entitlements every eligible Zambian citizen has when participating in an election, protected under the Constitution and electoral laws, including the right to register and vote if eligible, the right to a secret ballot, and the right to vote free from intimidation. Real-life application: discusses how a voter in Mkushi turned away from a polling station without valid reason, or forced to reveal who they voted for, has the right to report this to ECZ officials or election monitors present.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes on voters' rights. In pairs, they identify which right is being violated in short given cases (e.g. a farm supervisor telling employees who to vote for, or a presiding officer refusing a registered voter entry without reason), correctly identifying such cases as violations of the right to vote freely if eligible/registered. Assessment criteria: learners correctly identify the specific voter right violated in each case.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: at a large farm near Mkushi, the owner gathered workers before the by-election and told them he would only renew contracts for those who could prove they voted for his preferred candidate; one worker, Musonda, felt pressured but later reported the matter to an ECZ monitor at the polling station, who assured her that her ballot was secret and recorded her complaint for investigation. Tasks: (a) identify the voter's right that the farm owner threatened to violate [3 marks]; (b) explain how the ECZ monitor's response protected Musonda's rights as a voter [7 marks]; role-play task — dramatise Musonda reporting the incident to the ECZ monitor, including the monitor explaining ballot secrecy, recording her statement, and advising her on further steps [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) the farm owner threatened Musonda's right to vote freely, without intimidation or coercion, and her right to a secret ballot [3]. (b) the monitor protected Musonda's rights by assuring her that her vote was secret, meaning the farm owner could not know who she voted for, removing the basis for his threat, and by recording her complaint upheld her right to report violations for investigation, reinforcing that voters are protected by law regardless of their employer's wishes [7].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly identify the rights at risk and explain the protective role of the monitor; the role-play accurately reflects a respectful, supportive rights-protection process. Level of difficulty: (a) Remembering (b) Analysing; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to discuss with a parent or guardian what they believe are the most important rights a voter has, and why: (a) record two voters' rights identified by the parent/guardian [3 marks]; (b) state one reason why one of these rights matters, in their own words [2 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners discuss with a family member and record findings in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit a written record showing genuine discussion and correct identification of voters' rights.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'Every Zambian voter has rights that protect their choice — from the secrecy of the ballot to the freedom from pressure — and these rights make democracy meaningful.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state one voter's right they will remember. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly state at least one voter's right.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.2 Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) — Analysing Electoral Malpractice in Zambia
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Analysing electoral malpractice in Zambia
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to analyse forms of electoral malpractice in Zambia and their consequences.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, newspaper report on an electoral petition case.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson concludes Sub-topic 2.2.2 by equipping learners with critical thinking skills to identify and evaluate threats to electoral integrity, using Zambianised case examples. This is the 12th lesson in the series of 15.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.2.2.1 Analyse the role of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ)
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand voters' rights and the Electoral Code of Conduct (previous lessons).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks whether learners have heard of a Zambian election result being challenged in court, and why this happens.
progression.learnersRole: Learners share what they know or have heard, recalling election petitions on the news and suspecting reasons like rigging, vote-buying or violence. Assessment criteria: learners engage and share relevant prior knowledge or reasonable guesses.

progression.teacherRole: Defines electoral malpractice as any dishonest or illegal practice that undermines the fairness and credibility of an election, and outlines common forms in Zambia: vote-buying/bribery, ballot stuffing or tampering, intimidation and political violence, multiple voting or impersonation, misuse of government resources for campaigning, and manipulation of results. Real-life application: notes that election petitions have led courts to nullify constituency/council seat results after malpractice such as bribery or violence was proven.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes on forms of malpractice. In groups, they are given short case descriptions and must classify the type of malpractice involved and suggest one consequence — e.g. correctly classifying a candidate's agent giving out chitenge cloth for votes as vote-buying. Assessment criteria: learners correctly classify malpractice cases and identify a reasonable consequence.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: after the Mkushi North by-election result was announced, the losing candidate filed a High Court petition alleging that the winning candidate's agents had bribed voters in Katanino Ward with chitenge material and bags of sugar, and had inflated the number of votes recorded at one polling station beyond the number of registered voters there; the Court ordered a recount and investigation. Tasks: (a) identify two forms of electoral malpractice alleged in the scenario [4 marks]; (b) analyse the possible consequences for the winning candidate if the allegations are proven true [6 marks]; role-play task — dramatise a High Court hearing of the election petition, with roles for the petitioner's lawyer presenting evidence, the respondent's lawyer defending the candidate, and a judge delivering a reasoned ruling [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) forms alleged — vote-buying (distributing chitenge and sugar); ballot/vote tampering (inflated vote numbers beyond registered voters, suggesting ballot stuffing) [4]. (b) if proven, the court could nullify the result in the affected ward/constituency requiring a fresh by-election, disqualify the winning candidate for a specified period, expose the candidate and agents to criminal prosecution under the Electoral Process Act, and damage public trust in the wider electoral system [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly identify forms of malpractice and analyse realistic consequences; the role-play demonstrates a fair, reasoned judicial process. Level of difficulty: (a) Remembering (b) Analysing; role-play: Evaluating.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to find, from a newspaper, radio bulletin or an elder, one real or reported case of electoral malpractice in Zambia (local or national) and its outcome: (a) record the form of malpractice reported [2 marks]; (b) record the outcome or consequence that followed, if known [3 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners research at home and record findings in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit a relevant, accurately recorded case of electoral malpractice and its outcome.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'Electoral malpractice, whether bribery or tampering, threatens the very trust that elections are built on — and Zambia's laws and courts stand ready to correct it.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state one form of electoral malpractice they will remember and its consequence. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly state at least one form of electoral malpractice and a possible consequence.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.3 Electoral Systems — Examining Electoral Systems (Part 1: Single Member Plurality/Majoritarian System)
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Examining electoral systems (Part 1: Single Member Plurality/Majoritarian System)
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to examine the Single Member Plurality (Win-Takes-It-All) System and the Majoritarian System of elections.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, sample vote-count table.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson splits the compacted 'examining electoral systems' learning activity into a focused segment on the two majority-based systems, developing analytical and critical thinking through Zambianised illustrations. This is the 13th lesson in the series of 15.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand electoral malpractice and voters' rights (previous lessons).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher presents a simple vote count for a constituency election (Candidate A 4,000, Candidate B 3,500, Candidate C 2,500) and asks who should win and whether the winner needs more than half of all votes.
progression.learnersRole: Learners calculate and discuss, noting Candidate A has the most votes but not more than half of the total, sparking debate on whether that should be enough to win. Assessment criteria: learners engage with the numbers and reason about what should determine a winner.

progression.teacherRole: Explains the Single Member Plurality System ('Win-Takes-It-All'), where the candidate with the most votes in a constituency/ward wins even without an outright majority, and the Majoritarian System, where a candidate must win more than 50% (an absolute majority) of votes cast, otherwise a second ballot is required between the top candidates.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes copying both systems' rules. In pairs, they are given different vote totals for a hypothetical Mkushi ward election and determine the winner under each system, showing that the outcome can differ depending on which system is used. Assessment criteria: learners correctly apply both systems to determine winners from given vote data.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: in a mock Katanino Ward Council election organised by the school's Civic Education Club, three candidates received votes — Mumba 180, Zulu 150, Phiri 90, out of 420 votes cast in total. Tasks: (a) determine the winner if the Single Member Plurality System is applied, giving a reason [4 marks]; (b) determine what would happen if the Majoritarian System were applied instead, giving a reason [6 marks]; role-play task — dramatise the Civic Education Club's mock election results announcement, with a Returning Officer first announcing the Single Member Plurality outcome, then explaining what would happen under the Majoritarian System [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) under Single Member Plurality, Mumba wins with 180 votes, because this system declares the candidate with the highest number of votes the winner regardless of whether it is more than half of the total [4]. (b) under the Majoritarian System, no candidate would win outright since none received more than 210 votes (over half of 420); a second ballot (run-off) would be needed between the top two candidates, Mumba (180) and Zulu (150) [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly apply both systems to the scenario's vote figures with sound reasoning; the role-play clearly distinguishes the outcomes under each system. Level of difficulty: (a) Applying (b) Analysing; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to create their own hypothetical vote totals for three candidates in a fictitious Zambian ward, then apply both systems: (a) state their invented vote totals and determine the Single Member Plurality winner [3 marks]; (b) determine whether a run-off would be needed under the Majoritarian System, and why [2 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners create and solve their own hypothetical example at home, recording the working in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit a correctly worked hypothetical example showing understanding of both systems.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'Under Single Member Plurality, the most votes is enough to win; under the Majoritarian System, a candidate must clear the higher bar of more than half — the choice of system can change who becomes the leader.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state, in one sentence, the difference between the two systems. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly distinguish the Single Member Plurality System from the Majoritarian System.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.3 Electoral Systems — Examining Electoral Systems (Part 2: Proportional Representation and Mixed Member Proportionality Systems)
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Examining electoral systems (Part 2: Proportional Representation and Mixed Member Proportionality Systems)
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to examine the Proportional Representation System and the Mixed Member Proportionality System of elections.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026).
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, sample party-vote-share table.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson completes the 'examining electoral systems' learning activity by covering the remaining two systems, developing analytical thinking and collaboration through comparative, Zambianised group work. This is the 14th lesson in the series of 15.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the Single Member Plurality and Majoritarian Systems (previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks whether it is fair for a political party that gets 30% of the national vote to get 30% of the seats in Parliament, rather than none at all.
progression.learnersRole: Learners discuss and share opinions; most agree it seems fairer, though some are unsure how such a system would work in practice. Assessment criteria: learners engage with the fairness question and offer a reasoned opinion.

progression.teacherRole: Explains the Proportional Representation System, in which legislative seats are allocated to parties in proportion to their percentage of votes nationally or regionally, rather than through individual constituency contests, and the Mixed Member Proportionality System, which combines constituency-based elections with proportional representation — some legislators elected directly, others allocated to correct imbalance — unlike Zambia's current First-Past-the-Post system for MPs, where winning individual constituencies is what matters regardless of national vote share.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take notes comparing the two systems. In groups, they are given a table of a fictitious country's party vote shares (e.g. Party X 45%, Party Y 35%, Party Z 20%) and calculate how many of 100 seats each party would receive under pure Proportional Representation. Assessment criteria: learners correctly calculate proportional seat allocation from given vote-share data (e.g. Party X 45 seats, Party Y 35 seats, Party Z 20 seats).

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: the fictitious neighbouring country of Kalobwe uses a Mixed Member Proportionality System for its National Assembly — half of the 100 seats are won directly by constituency candidates (like Zambia's First-Past-the-Post MPs), while the other half are allocated to parties based on national vote share to correct any imbalance; in the last election the Unity Front won 30 constituency seats but only 35% of the national vote. Tasks: (a) explain how Kalobwe's Mixed Member Proportionality System works, using scenario details [4 marks]; (b) analyse how the proportional seats could adjust the Unity Front's final seat total to better reflect their national vote share [6 marks]; role-play task — dramatise Kalobwe's Electoral Commission announcing the final seat allocation, with an officer explaining to party representatives how the proportional 'top-up' seats were calculated [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) Kalobwe's system combines directly-elected constituency seats with additional seats allocated based on national vote share, so the final Assembly composition better reflects how the whole country voted [4]. (b) since Unity Front won 30 constituency seats (30% of the 100-seat Assembly) but received 35% of the national vote, proportional seats would be allocated to bring their overall seat share closer to 35, correcting the 5-percentage-point gap [6].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly explain the Mixed Member Proportionality System and reason through the seat adjustment; the role-play accurately conveys the allocation logic. Level of difficulty: (a) Understanding (b) Analysing; role-play: Applying.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to research (from a library book, newspaper or the internet where accessible) one country that uses Proportional Representation or Mixed Member Proportionality (e.g. South Africa, Germany) and note one feature of how it works: (a) record the name of the country and system used [2 marks]; (b) record one feature of how the system works in that country [3 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners research at home and record findings in their notebooks. Assessment criteria: learners submit accurate, relevant research findings on a real country's electoral system.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher concludes: 'Proportional Representation shares seats according to votes won nationally, while Mixed Member Proportionality blends this fairness with the direct link constituencies provide — different systems, different balances of fairness.'
progression.learnersRole: Learners state one difference between Proportional Representation and Mixed Member Proportionality. Assessment criteria: learners can correctly distinguish the two systems in their own words.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 2.2.3 Electoral Systems — Explaining Zambia's Electoral System (Majoritarian System for President/Vice-President and First-Past-the-Post for National Assembly and Local Government)
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Explaining Zambia's electoral system (Majoritarian System for President/Vice-President and First-Past-the-Post for National Assembly and Local Government)
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to explain the electoral system Zambia actually uses for Presidential, National Assembly and Local Government elections, as provided under the Republican Constitution and the Electoral Process Act.
lesson_plans.references: Civic Education Syllabus Ordinary Level Secondary Education Form 1-4 (2024), page 42; ECSEOL Assessment Schemes for Civic Education 3011 (ECZ, 2026); Republican Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 2 of 2016; Electoral Process Act No. 35 of 2016.
lesson_plans.tlm: Whiteboard, markers, diagram of Zambia's electoral structure for President, MP and Councillor.
lesson_plans.rationale: This final lesson under Topic 2.2 applies all prior knowledge of electoral systems specifically to Zambia's own constitutional arrangement, consolidating learners' understanding through Zambianised, real election-result examples. This is the 15th and final lesson in the series.
objectives: Specific competence: 2.3.1.1 Explain Zambia's electoral system
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the Single Member Plurality, Majoritarian, Proportional Representation and Mixed Member Proportionality Systems (previous lessons).

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks how Zambia actually elects its own President, and whether the same system is used for MPs.
progression.learnersRole: Learners recall the systems learnt and try to guess which applies to Zambia's President and MPs; some correctly recall that the President needs more than 50% while MPs simply need the most votes, though many need confirmation. Assessment criteria: learners actively attempt to apply prior knowledge to the Zambian context.

progression.teacherRole: Explains that the 2016 Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act and the Electoral Process Act clearly define Zambia's electoral system: the President and Vice-President are elected using the Majoritarian (50%+1) System, while MPs and Local Government Councillors are elected using the First-Past-the-Post (Single Member Plurality) System — the candidate with the highest votes in their constituency/ward wins without needing more than 50%. Real-life application: explains the rationale — the 50%+1 rule for the presidency ensures broad national support given the power of the office, while First-Past-the-Post for MPs and Councillors is simpler and creates a direct link between a representative and their specific constituency or ward, such as Mkushi North Constituency or Chalata Ward.
progression.learnersRole: Learners listen and take detailed notes, copying the diagram from the board, and ask questions (e.g. about ballot procedures). Assessment criteria: learners can correctly state which electoral system is used for the President and which for MPs/Councillors, and explain the reason for the difference.

progression.teacherRole: Scenario: in the 2021 Zambian general elections, President Hakainde Hichilema was declared winner of the presidential race after securing more than 50% of the valid votes cast nationally; in the same elections, in Mkushi North Constituency the winning parliamentary candidate secured victory with 38% of the vote ahead of two rivals splitting the remainder, while in Chalata Ward the winning Councillor won by just 300 votes more than the closest competitor. Tasks: (a) identify the electoral system used to elect the President in the scenario, giving evidence [3 marks]; (b) identify and explain the electoral system used to elect the MP and the Councillor in the scenario [7 marks]; role-play task — dramatise an ECZ results announcement ceremony, with an officer separately announcing the presidential result (explaining the 50%+1 requirement), the Mkushi North MP result (explaining First-Past-the-Post), and the Chalata Ward Councillor result, clarifying to a curious first-time voter why the rules differ [10 marks]. Expected answers: (a) the Majoritarian System (50%+1) was used, as the President needed to secure more than 50% of the valid votes cast nationally [3]. (b) the First-Past-the-Post (Single Member Plurality) System was used for both the MP and Councillor — shown because the MP won with only 38% (not more than half), simply having more votes than each individual rival, and similarly the Councillor won by a 300-vote margin without needing to cross the 50% threshold; this system is used for MPs and Councillors because it is simpler to administer across many constituencies/wards and creates a direct, accountable link between each representative and their area [7].
progression.learnersRole: Learners correctly identify and explain both systems as applied to the scenario with accurate reasoning; the role-play clearly and correctly distinguishes the rules for each type of election. Level of difficulty: (a) Remembering (b) Analysing; role-play: Evaluating.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher asks learners to research (from a newspaper, radio bulletin, or ECZ website where accessible) the vote result for their own constituency's MP or ward's Councillor: (a) record the vote result found for their MP or Councillor [2 marks]; (b) state which electoral system this confirms was used, giving one reason [3 marks].
progression.learnersRole: Learners research the vote result at home and record findings. Assessment criteria: learners submit a correctly recorded result and correctly identify the electoral system it confirms was used.

progression.teacherRole: The teacher draws two columns on the board, 'President' and 'MP/Councillor,' and asks the class to chorally state the correct electoral system for each column.
progression.learnersRole: Learners respond chorally: 'Majoritarian, 50%+1!' for President, and 'First-Past-the-Post!' for MP/Councillor. Assessment criteria: learners can confidently and correctly name the two electoral systems used in Zambia and the offices to which each applies, consolidating the entire Topic 2.2 on Elections.
